articles.title: Nepal floods: 117 tourists rescued, 85 Indians among them; death toll rises over 500
articles.summary: South Asia News: A total of 117 tourists have been rescued from flood-hit areas of Nepal, including 85 Indians, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Friday, as rescue opera.
articles.body: A total of 117 tourists have been rescued from flood-hit areas of Nepal, including 85 Indians, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Friday, as rescue operations continued for a third day following devastating flash floods.The rescued tourists include 16 Chinese nationals, nine from South Korea, two each from the US and Italy, while the identities of three others are yet to be confirmed, according to news agency ANI.The flash floods that swept through Rasuwa and other parts of central Nepal on Wednesday have killed at least 538 people, while nearly 1,000 others remain missing, the Associated Press reported citing officials. The disaster caused widespread damage to settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower projects.Nepal Police said 1,545 injured and stranded people have been rescued so far, while 7,451 security personnel have been deployed for search-and-rescue operations.Among those rescued, 84 people are currently receiving treatment at hospitals in Kathmandu. Helicopters have been deployed to reach isolated areas and evacuate survivors, while ground teams continue searching riverbanks and downstream settlements.Police said 977 people, including 86 security personnel, 517 foreign tourists and 127 Nepali travellers, are still missing.Fresh flood threat after barrier lake formsAuthorities have also warned of a possible second wave of flooding after a rise in the water level of a newly formed barrier lake near the Nepal-Tibet border.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said the rising water level at the site of Wednesday's flash flood had increased the risk of further flooding."The water level mixed with mud has increased at the same place where the flash flood occurred on Wednesday, and there is a risk of more flooding in the area," the NDRRMA said in a fresh notice.The authority urged people involved in rescue operations and those staying in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli areas to remain highly alert and move to safer locations if necessary.Nepal Police also issued a warning after receiving information that a water dam on the Tibetan side had burst again."Information has been received that the water dam on the Tibetan side has burst again," Nepal Police said in a post on X.According to Nepal Police, 178 bodies have been recovered from Chitwan, 110 from Nawalparasi East, 44 from Gorkha, 37 from Nuwakot and 33 from Dhading.Another 28 bodies were recovered from Tanahu, 27 from Nawalparasi West and 12 from Rasuwa. Three people were also reported killed in neighbouring Tibet.China issued a Level-IV emergency alert late Thursday after a large barrier lake formed near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers near the Nepal-Tibet border.Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology had earlier warned of a fresh flood risk downstream of the Bhotekoshi River following the formation of the lake.Chinese authorities informed Nepal that around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated in the lake, with another 3 million cubic metres potentially entering it over three days, raising concerns about a possible breach.The lake formed near rivers originating in Tibet that flow into Nepal as part of the Bhotekoshi river system.Meanwhile, the Nepal government has decided to suspend all examinations from August 29 in view of the situation following the natural disaster.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jersey shepherds say GPS technology making lives 'much easier'
articles.summary: Brothers Josh and Ben Voak are using a GPS technology featured on the TV show Clarkson's Farm.
articles.body:
GPS collars are changing the way animals grazing on Jersey's cliffsides are managed, local shepherds have said.

Conservation initiative The Grazing Project has pioneered use of the collars on large flocks of sheep, with its efforts so successful it is now training four grazing cows to use the collars too.

In 2025, the technology was featured on Clarkson's Farm, Jeremy Clarkson's fly-on-the-wall documentary about his Cotswolds farm Diddly Squat, where it was used to contain his herd of goats.

Jersey brothers and shepherds Josh and Ben Voak, who work with the project, said it had saved them hours of manual labour and opened up new areas for flocks to graze.

The collars use GPS technology to keep livestock within an invisible boundary drawn using a smartphone app.

If the animals reach the edge of the boundary the collar delivers an audio warning and then delivers mild electric shocks.

The technology was created in Norway and has been tested extensively across the UK. The project uses about 150 collars as part of its management of 600 sheep in Jersey.

Josh said: "We got our first 70 collars about three years ago now, since then we've been getting more and more because it makes our job so much easier.

"It means we can graze more challenging areas, so steep cliffs, areas with heavy bracken or gorse... it means we can also track the sheep as well, so every day when we go looking and counting the sheep we've got them already on the app and we can find them very easily."

"We used to lay electric fencing before the GPS collars came in," he added.

"That means lugging fence poles, wire, batteries up and down the cliff. It could take hours.

"But now with the GPS collars all we have to do is upload the site on to the app, put sheep in and then we're done."

Ben said The Grazing Project was "quite pioneering" in the sheer number of collars it uses.

He said: "We certainly speak to a lot of people about it and they're very interested.

"For a lot of farmers who do struggle with sheep who love to escape, it can be a really useful tool.

"We speak to Nofence a lot about the design of the collar itself and how to improve that because if we ever come across an issue they're really good at taking in that feedback, learning it and sending us maybe a new type of chain or a new type of strap that can increase how usable it is."

Ben said training cows to wear the collars had opened up the possibility of using sheep and cows together to rewild new parts of Jersey.

He said: "They're currently being trained at the farm as we speak and the plan is to put them on certain wetland sites or up on the north coast, not letting them on the cliffs.

"We're in a trial period seeing how the cows and the sheep work together, if we can put the collars with cows and sheep on the same site, so it's quite an exciting time for us because we're just testing those possibilities."

articles.title: Scarborough's Capitol Plaza recognised as community asset
articles.summary: The former Scarborough cinema is formally recognised as plans for a theatre revival progress.
articles.body:
Scarborough's Capitol Plaza has been recognised as an asset of community value by North Yorkshire Council.

The Grade II listed venue on Albemarle Crescent opened in 1929 as the town's first "talkie" cinema and later became home to Mecca Bingo.

The Capitol Theatre Trust hopes to transform the building into a receiving house theatre capable of hosting major touring productions alongside a range of community facilities.

Trust director George Wakely said: "Just as Mecca Bingo once served as a lifeline for the community, we want the Capitol to continue that legacy."

North Yorkshire Council confirmed the successful nomination on Tuesday.

The designation recognises the venue's community value and could give the community an opportunity to bid for the building if it is put up for sale.

Plans for the building include a community cafe, accessible facilities, low-cost rehearsal and meeting rooms and creative workspaces.

A public consultation is due to begin on 19 September.

Wakely said: "Whilst we're fortunate to have strong cultural venues like the Open Air Theatre, the Stephen Joseph Theatre and the Spa, none can accommodate the scale or technical requirements of major UK tours.

"Our aim isn't to compete with existing venues, but to complement them with something Scarborough currently lacks."

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , Scarborough once had 11 theatres and music halls, but only four remain in operation.

The Capitol later became a Mecca Bingo hall, which occupied the building from 1977 until it closed amid concerns about its condition.

Following a site visit in July, council officers said the venue was "well-known within the local area", had historic and cultural significance and continued to attract support from residents.

Officers added that the trust's proposals appeared "positive in principle" and aligned with community-focused objectives.

Wakely said the trust hoped to complete the final phase of the redevelopment and reopen the venue in October 2029, 100 years after the Capitol first opened its doors.

articles.title: Colman's Mustard brand synonymous with Norwich put up for sale
articles.summary: The sale comes before a proposed merger between parent company Unilever and McCormick.
articles.body:
A famous mustard brand synonymous with Norwich has been put up for sale.

Colman's Mustard, which had a factory in Norwich for 160 years, has been put on the market ahead of a merger between Unilever and American food giant McCormick in a deal believed to be worth £48bn.

The company has been deeply rooted in Norfolk after it was founded in 1814 by Jeremiah Colman at Stoke Holy Cross before production moved to Carrow in 1858.

A Unilever spokesperson said: "A decision has been taken to market the Colman's brand and assets to potential buyers in order to proactively seek to address potential competition concerns from the planned combination of Unilever Foods and McCormick."

Based outside of Norwich, the firm had a cradle-to-grave ethos and provided education, housing, healthcare and leisure for workers and their families.

A school was built on Carrow Hill in 1864 for employees' children and the firm supplied coffins for workers and their families, and built a series of terrace houses which were believed to have doors painted mustard yellow.

In January 2018, Unilever announced it would close the Carrow plant and the last jar of mustard rolled off the production line in 2019 before the factory was closed in 2020.

The 42-acre (17 hectare) site has sat empty since it closed and has been earmarked for thousands of homes.

Unilever shifted manufacturing to Burton-on-Trent and Germany.

Condimentum, based at the Food Enterprise Park in Easton, near Norwich, had been keeping Colman's Norwich legacy alive by producing the raw material for the brand.

The wider deal will see McCormick take control of household names including Hellmann's, Marmite, Knorr and Pot Noodle.

The American food giant already owns French's — one of the world's biggest rival mustard brands.

While Unilever will focus on home and personal care with brands including Dove, Persil and Lynx.

A Unilever spokesperson said discussions are ongoing and operations continue as usual.

articles.title: LA merchants fight to save 97-year-old cross as lawyer warns of nationwide stakes
articles.summary: Olvera Street merchants ask the Ninth Circuit to defend a nearly century-old cross and Nativity display an atheist lawsuit targets in Los Angeles.
articles.body: A legal battle over a nearly century-old cross tradition and longstanding Nativity display in the historic heart of Los Angeles could threaten generations of Mexican-American traditions and leave religious monuments across the country vulnerable, an attorney representing local merchants fighting to preserve the displays told Fox News Digital. "If the cross and nativity were taken down, it would just be the first step in unraveling the vibrant community cultural celebrations, a lot of which have their roots in Mexican-American Catholic history and really decimating this tight-knit community," Andrea Butler, counsel at Becket and lead attorney for the merchants, told Fox News Digital Thursday in an interview. A cross has stood at the head of Olvera Street since 1929, when the original was raised to celebrate Los Angeles' 148th birthday, while a life-size Nativity is displayed each December as part of the community's traditional Las Posadas celebration. SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING Last year, according to Becket, a resident sued the city asking it to remove or cover the cross and stop the Nativity display, arguing the display "offends [him] and makes [him] feel excluded as a non-believer." The religious-liberty group said merchants have helped preserve those traditions since the area was revitalized in the 1920s, with some current vendors belonging to families that have operated at the market since it opened in 1930. Merchants also help organize annual cultural and religious celebrations, including Día de los Reyes, Día de los Muertos and Las Posadas. In its Monday filing, Becket asked the Ninth Circuit to allow the Olvera Street Merchants Association Foundation to join the legal battle over a nearly century-old cross and longstanding Nativity display at El Pueblo in Los Angeles. Becket said the merchants are seeking to defend religious and cultural traditions their families have helped preserve for generations. According to Becket, El Pueblo attracts millions of visitors each year to its Olvera Street marketplace, historic sites and cultural events celebrating the neighborhood’s Mexican-American heritage. YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE "El Pueblo and Olvera Street are some of the most historic areas in Los Angeles," Butler said. "They are very near the site of the original founding of the city back in the 1700s, and the area has had a long and sometimes bumpy history throughout the history of LA. It… went through substantial decline for centuries, and then in the 1930s, the historic and cultural value of the area was really recognized, and there was a concerted effort to restore the area, preserve the city's historical and cultural history through designating it as El Pueblo Historical Monument. And at the time of the 1930s when the restoration efforts were really underway, that's when the Olvera Street Market took shape, and our clients, the merchants, are members of families who have been selling their goods on the market on Olvera Street since the 1930s." Butler added, "Most of them are third or fourth generation members of this community. And so the cross and the nativity are really vital components of long-standing history and tradition, most of which, in the context of El Pueblo, is Mexican-American history really celebrated in Los Angeles culture." She said the case is about whether the First Amendment will be upheld in protecting the displays. "At the Becket Fund, we believe that religion is a natural part of human culture and history, and it's something that should be celebrated just like any other part of our heritage, history, culture, and it's not something that needs to be basically thought of as kind of a dirty word or something that needs to be taken down because some people might find it offensive," Butler said. "It's something that is a natural part of human culture and should be part of the displays that we see celebrating our culture throughout the country," she added. "And the idea that the founders would have thought a passive religious display celebrating a historical moment in time needed to be taken down because it violated the First Amendment is really absurd." FEDERAL COURT UPHOLDS TEXAS LAW REQUIRING TEN COMMANDMENTS IN PUBLIC CLASSROOMS In a statement to Fox News Digital, Valerie Hanley, treasurer of the Olvera Street Merchants Association Foundation, said, "Olvera Street is not just a part of our families’ heritage, it’s at the heart of Los Angeles’s history. One offended bystander shouldn’t get to decide which parts of our City’s story we can tell." Fox News Digital reached out Jack Gerritsen, one of the plaintiffs in the case, for comment. articles.title: Wind farm planned close to Flow Country World Heritage Site
articles.summary: The developer says its project involves up to 12 turbines and would see the restoration of peatbog.
articles.body:
Plans for up to 12 wind turbines near the Flow Country World Heritage Site in the Highlands have been submitted to the Scottish government.

Low Carbon said its Forsinain Forest Wind Farm, proposed for land 2 miles (3km) north of Forsinard, would be "fully outwith" the Unesco-designated site.

It said the project include proposals to restore 383 acres of non-native forest to peatbog.

The world heritage site covers almost 469,500 acres of one of the most intact and extensive blanket bog systems in the world.

Unesco status was achieved for the Flow Country, which includes parts of Caithness and Sutherland, in July 2024 after an almost 40-year campaign .

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Low Carbon had planned up to 19 turbines but reduced the number during a series of "design refinements".

The company said the project could generate enough electricity to power more than 98,000 homes each year.

It added that a community benefit fund associated with the wind farm could be worth about £432,000 per year, and the project could provide an estimated £1m annually in business rates for Highland Council.

Andy Sloan, project development director at Low Carbon, said: "Forsinain Forest is a key part of our growing pipeline of onshore wind in Scotland, which if approved, will support Scottish climate targets, help accelerate the UK's transition to clean energy and bolster energy security by reducing our reliance on fossil fuels.

"By combining clean energy generation with nature restoration and long-term community benefit, Forsinain Forest can help to deliver lasting economic value for the communities that host it."

The Flow Country's rare blanket bog ecosystem supports a range of notable species including a host of sphagnum mosses and other wetland plants.

There are all sorts of insects and a host of rare birds including greenshank, golden plover, dunlin and hen harrier.

The Flow Country Partnership has been contacted for comment.

RSPB Scotland, which manages a reserve at Forsinard, said it was supportive of "carefully sited" renewable energy schemes.

A spokesperson said: "We have just been consulted on the full application for Forsinain Forest Wind Farm and will be carefully considering the proposed development.

"However, we do have significant concerns over a wind farm at this very sensitive location for nature, in the heart of The Flow Country Unesco World Heritage Site, adjacent to nationally and internationally protected sites for nature and RSPB's Forsinard Flows Nature Reserve."

articles.title: FM calls for referendum powers as draft independence bill published
articles.summary: The draft bill would be introduced into Parliament if the Scottish government secured the necessary powers from the UK government.
articles.body:
The Scottish government has published its draft independence referendum bill, setting out the details of the proposed question and who would be allowed to vote.

The short document has been released ahead of the first minister setting out his legislative plans for the year on Tuesday.

John Swinney called on the UK government to "respect the voice of the Scottish people and parliament and transfer the necessary powers" in order to hold the vote.

Since 2014 successive UK governments have opposed any further referendums and Downing Street recently said a fresh poll was "off limits" .

A UK government spokesperson said: "The prime minister made clear to the first minister in their first meeting that another referendum on independence was off the table. It would take our focus away from growing the economy and helping families with the cost of living.

"We will continue working with the Scottish government and other partners to build a fairer country for everyone."

Burnham tells Swinney independence is 'off limits' at Commonwealth Games meeting

Scotland previously voted against becoming an independent country by 55% to 45%.

In 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled that any further vote would require the agreement of the UK government.

The proposed ballot paper for a second referendum would ask: "Should Scotland be an independent country?" and voters would mark an "X" against options Yes or No.

The draft bill would be introduced into parliament if the Scottish government secured approval from the UK government.

The document would include a date for the referendum once it was put before Holyrood.

The SNP had promised to publish the draft legislation in their first 100 days in government after the Scottish election in May.

Swinney said: "The world has changed fundamentally since 2014. So has the UK, and so has Scotland.

"Scotland is ready. The Scottish people are ready. It is time the UK government delivered."

The first minister said he would have "more to say about Scotland's constitutional future in the coming weeks".

He added: "Fundamentally, nobody will take better decisions about Scotland's future than the people who live here.

"That future belongs to the people of Scotland - and no-one else."

In line with current legislation, registered voters over the age of 16, as well as qualifying foreign nationals, would be able to vote in a second referendum.

Earlier this year, Prof Sir John Curtice of Strathclyde University said Scotland remained "more or less divided down the middle on the subject".

He added: "Sometimes yes is a little ahead of no, sometimes it's the other way around. Yes is typically stronger than it was in the actual referendum."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Swinney ahead of the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony in Glasgow last month.

Afterwards a Downing Street statement said: "The prime minister stated up front that another referendum on independence was off limits because it would take our focus away from growing the economy and helping families with the cost of living."

Scottish Labour acting leader Jackie Baillie said: "The people of Scotland deserve far better than this failing SNP government that is more interested in empty gestures and grandstanding than it is in improving the lives of people across the country."

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay called on Swinney to "abandon this tedious obsession and get on with the day job."

articles.title: A young German tourist stole a human skull from Vienna’s cathedral catacombs and kept it for about 60 years; near the end of his life, he mailed it back with a confession
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For around six decades, a human skull taken from the catacombs beneath Vienna's St. Stephen's Cathedral remained far from its original resting place. .
articles.body: For around six decades, a human skull taken from the catacombs beneath Vienna's St. Stephen's Cathedral remained far from its original resting place. The skull had reportedly been stolen by a young German tourist during a visit to the cathedral's underground burial chambers and kept for much of his life. Then, near the end of his life, the man decided to return it. According to a report by the Austrian newspaper Krone, the skull unexpectedly arrived back at St. Stephen's Cathedral in a parcel, accompanied by a letter from an elderly man in northern Germany. In the letter, he confessed that he had taken the skull as a young tourist around 60 years earlier and said that, as his life was drawing to a close, he wanted to make peace with himself. The extraordinary return brought an end to a story that had apparently begun with an act of youthful recklessness and concluded decades later with an attempt at remorse and restitution.An unexpected packageThe unusual discovery began when Franz Zehetner, an official associated with St. Stephen's Cathedral, found a large, tied parcel on his desk without a specific sender. What appeared at first to be an ordinary mysterious package turned out to contain something far more startling: a human skull. Inside was also a letter explaining how it had ended up there. The elderly man who sent the parcel wrote that he had stolen the skull while visiting the cathedral's catacombs as a young German tourist. After keeping it for approximately 60 years, he had decided to send it back.According to Krone, the man wrote that he had reached the end of his life and wanted to settle his conscience. The confession transformed the strange package from an unexplained discovery into the conclusion of a decades-old theft. Zehetner was reportedly moved by the gesture, despite the extraordinary circumstances surrounding the skull's disappearance and return.A decades-old theftThe theft reportedly took place during a guided visit to the catacombs beneath St. Stephen's Cathedral, one of Vienna's best-known landmarks. The underground chambers contain the remains of thousands of people and form an important part of the cathedral's history. For the young visitor, however, one of those human remains became an unusual and inappropriate souvenir. For decades, the skull remained outside the cathedral. There is little information about where it was kept during those years or why the man waited so long before returning it. What is known from his letter is that the decision came when he was elderly and reflecting on his life.The return also raised an obvious question: to whom had the skull belonged? Unfortunately, experts could not determine the identity of the person whose skull was taken or match it with other remains in the cathedral's catacombs. According to the reports, the catacombs contain remains from different periods of Vienna's history, including bones associated with secondary burials. As a result, the identity of the person whose skull was removed may never be known. After its return, however, the remains were finally given a dignified resting place.Back where it belongedThe catacombs beneath St. Stephen's Cathedral represent a hidden layer of Vienna's long history and contain the remains of countless people. Its owner remains unknown, and the circumstances of the person's original death and burial may never be established.What is known is that the remains became separated from their original resting place when a young visitor decided to take them away. Six decades later, they found their way back. Zehetner viewed the man's eventual decision to return the skull as more than simply correcting an old mistake. After approximately 60 years away from the cathedral, the remains were finally returned and laid to rest again.A final act of remorseThe story is unusual not only because of what was stolen, but because of how long the man apparently carried the consequences of his decision. According to his confession, the skull had remained away from the cathedral for most of his adult life. His identity has not been publicly revealed, leaving his letter as the only known account of the theft.What began, according to the man's confession, as a reckless act during a tourist visit eventually ended with an anonymous parcel, a written confession and the return of human remains that had been away from the cathedral for around 60 years. For the unknown person whose skull was taken, the journey finally came to an end beneath the same cathedral from which it had disappeared. And for the man who stole it, sending the skull back appears to have been a final attempt to make peace with a decision he had made when he was young.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Free climber stranded on Georgia rock face calls 911, prompting dramatic rescue by firefighter
articles.summary: Drone video captures firefighter Will Roper rappelling down Mount Yonah's cliff face to reach a free climber stranded on a tiny ledge 260 feet up.
articles.body: A free climber who called 911 after becoming stranded on a Georgia cliff face was rescued Tuesday by a firefighter who rappelled down to reach him. The climber, who hasn't been identified by authorities, was stuck on the west face of Mount Yonah, a 3,166-foot mountain ridge in the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest in North Georgia. According to White County Public Safety officials, the man called 911 at around 7 p.m. to report that he was unable to safely climb up or down the mountain. Authorities used a drone to locate the man, who was standing on a 20" by 20" ledge approximately 260 feet up the mountain. 11 VISITORS TRAPPED AS DANGEROUS FLASH FLOODING TEARS THROUGH ICONIC NATIONAL PARK White County firefighter Will Roper rappelled down the mountain to reach the man. Drone video showed Roper maneuvering beneath him before securing him in a harness and clipping him to the rope. The climber was then hoisted to the top of the mountain. The entire rescue operation took about 42 minutes, officials said. Roper told FOX 5 Atlanta said this was the first time he's had to rescue someone on a mountain. FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT "I've done a lot with dummies and a lot with other firefighters in training, but that's the first time that I've ever done it, kind of in the heat of the moment with a live subject," Roper said. "It was a little nerve-racking going over the edge," he added. Roper said the climber was strikingly calm, telling FOX 5 he jokingly asked him: "Have you been rescued before? You're pretty good at this." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The climber told Roper that he had experience with Mount Yonah but simply picked the wrong route and got stuck. "I've been on kind of a high since then, just to have the first rescue," Roper said, adding that he was glad to be able to help someone using his technical training.

articles.title: Rwanda genocide: Dutch court sentences man to life over massacre
articles.summary: The court in The Hague convicted the 66-year-old of war crimes and the crime of genocide.
articles.body:
A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said.

Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen.

In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists.

The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda.

"The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes".

At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them.

Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said.

Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire.

"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said.

As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024.

N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events".

"The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide.

His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP.

articles.title: In 1856, one of Northern California’s oldest cattle ranches was established; 170 years later, its 14,177 acres are being bought for $15.5 million and opened to the public
articles.summary: US News: The Wildlands Conservancy has agreed to buy one of Northern California’s oldest working livestock operations, protecting 14,177 acres of historic wild.
articles.body: The Wildlands Conservancy has agreed to buy one of Northern California’s oldest working livestock operations, protecting 14,177 acres of historic wilderness in Siskiyou County and turning it into a huge public preserve. The $15.5 million purchase of the AP Ranch, detailed in reports by the San Francisco Chronicle and official documents from The Wildlands Conservancy, marks a major change for a landscape that has been privately owned for 170 years. Located in rural western Siskiyou County near Gazelle, the vast property will be combined with the existing 6,094-acre Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve. Once the deal is complete, the connected public preserve will cover more than 20,000 acres across the Scott River watershed. Founded in 1856 by Alexander Parker soon after the California Gold Rush, the AP Ranch is one of the region’s oldest continuously operating agricultural properties. The Newton family bought the estate in 1961 and later expanded it by purchasing nearby land. They ran the property as a year-round cow-calf operation with capacity for about 500 mother cows. According to listing details from California Outdoor Properties, the ranch has varied terrain centred around the prominent Lover’s Leap peak. Elevations range from about 3,600 feet to 5,400 feet, with the Marble Mountain Wilderness and Klamath National Forest forming the backdrop.Protecting headwaters and wildlife corridorsThe purchase is important not only because of the ranch’s history, but also because of its ecological value. The AP Ranch contains the headwaters of the East Fork of the Scott River, which runs freely for eight miles through the property. The Scott River provides important spawning habitat for wild Coho salmon, king salmon and steelhead trout. The deal also includes extensive adjudicated water rights on the East Fork and its tributaries, as well as rights connected to two alpine lakes, Kangaroo Lake and Rock Fence Lake. Conservationists hope these rights will help protect water flows during the dry summer months, when falling water levels can make it harder for migratory fish to survive and move through the watershed. The Wildlands Conservancy said the surrounding landscape is also an important link for wildlife moving through mixed-conifer forests, oak woodlands and alpine meadows. The expanded preserve will border thousands of acres of federal forest land and provide habitat for many native species, including Roosevelt elk, Columbia blacktail deer, black bears, mountain lions, wild turkeys and American goshawks. The area is also within the growing range of California’s recovering gray wolf packs. Rewilding work will focus on restoring habitats and supporting native wildlife. The Scott River basin is home to American beavers, a keystone species whose dams can slow water, restore floodplains and help recharge groundwater. The conservancy plans to work with local tribal and environmental groups, including the Quartz Valley Indian Reservation, the Karuk Tribe, the Lomakatsi Restoration Project, California Trout and the Scott River Watershed Council, to improve the health of the wider watershed.From working ranch to public preserveThe sale brings an end to more than six decades of ownership by the Newton family. Albert Newton III said the family had developed a deep personal connection to the land during its long tenure. “Over the years, the ranch has hosted everyone from dignitaries and politicians to our kids' college friends,” Newton said, highlighting the property’s role as a gathering place in the Scott Valley. The AP Ranch includes seven homes, six historic timber barns and large cattle corrals equipped with certified scales. Under the new plan, The Wildlands Conservancy will gradually end intensive commercial operations while developing facilities for public use. The non-profit organisation operates California’s largest private preserve system and welcomes more than 1.5 million visitors each year to protected areas across California and Utah, with no admission fee. The new preserve will offer free public access for activities such as hiking, wildlife watching and educational trips for local schools. Higher parts of the property have views towards Mount Shasta and will also offer opportunities for winter activities, including cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Fundraising is now underway. The Wildlands Conservancy is seeking private donations and public grants to cover the $15.5 million purchase and support long-term management, trail building and habitat restoration across the newly protected landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India buys 60 US Javelins for Rs 292 crore to boost anti-tank firepower - what it means
articles.summary: News News: India and the United States have signed a Rs 292-crore government-to-government deal for around 60 Javelin anti-tank guided missiles for the Indian Ar.
articles.body: India and the United States have signed a Rs 292-crore government-to-government deal for around 60 Javelin anti-tank guided missiles for the Indian Army, in a procurement aimed at strengthening the force's anti-armour capabilities after Operation Sindoor, defence sources told ANI.The missiles are being acquired under the sixth emergency procurement window (EP-6), which permits the armed forces to procure equipment worth up to Rs 300 crore per contract. The Javelin deal is therefore being placed in limited numbers, with deliveries under the emergency procurement contracts expected to begin by the end of 2026-27.The deal follows a public announcement by US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who said India planned to buy the “battle-tested” Javelin anti-tank system. Gor said the acquisition would deepen the US-India defence relationship and could also open the door to co-production opportunities between the two countries.What is the Javelin?The FGM-148 Javelin is a man-portable anti-tank guided missile system developed and produced by the Javelin Joint Venture of Lockheed Martin and RTX for the US military. It is designed primarily to destroy tanks and other armoured vehicles, but can also be used against bunkers, fortified positions, buildings and other battlefield targets.The system consists of a missile sealed inside a disposable launch tube and a reusable Command Launch Unit (CLU), which provides day and thermal imaging sights for target detection and engagement.The Javelin uses a passive imaging-infrared seeker and has a fire-and-forget capability. Once the operator locks on to a target and launches the missile, the seeker guides it without requiring the soldier to continuously control its flight. This allows the operator to quickly move to cover or change position after firing.The missile has a 127-mm diameter and weighs about 15.5 kg as a complete round, while the missile itself weighs around 11.8 kg. The reusable command launch unit weighs roughly 7 kg in the current configuration. The system can engage targets from around 65 metres to up to 4 km in most operational conditions.Another important feature is its soft-launch system. The missile is initially ejected from the launch tube before its main rocket motor ignites, allowing the Javelin to be fired from relatively confined positions. The system can be operated by infantry and can also be integrated with vehicles and other platforms.Javelin first saw during the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq. According to its manufacturers, Javelin had been used in more than 5,000 engagements in Iraq and Afghanistan.The missile gained renewed international prominence after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine had received Javelins from the US before the invasion and used them against Russian armoured forces during the early stages of the war

articles.title: Oslo mayor cancels own wedding after death of Norway's king
articles.summary: Anne Lindboe, the mayor of Norway's capital, had planned to marry her fiance on Friday.
articles.body:
Oslo's Mayor Anne Lindboe has called off her wedding ceremony because of the death of King Harald V of Norway.

The wedding with her fiancé Pål Sandvid was planned to take place on Friday but was postponed after the king died earlier the same day, her political adviser confirmed to the BBC.

"It's hard to imagine an Oslo and a Norway without you. You didn't need a crown to be king," Lindboe wrote in a tribute to the late monarch on Instagram.

Harald reigned for 35 years and died at the national hospital in Norway's capital, where he was being treated for a rare blood condition. His son, King Haakon VIII , ascended the throne on Friday.

Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises

"Even the majority of Norwegians who never met you in person still felt like they knew you," Lindboe added in her tribute.

No new date has been set for the wedding yet, Lindboe's political adviser said.

After five years together, Lindboe announced the couple's engagement in June this year.

The late king was a popular and reforming leader in Norway who modernised the monarchy.

He broke with tradition by marrying a commoner, Queen Sonja, and served as a unifying figure during Norway's most difficult moments.

Harald died a day before their 58th wedding anniversary.

Members of the public have been gathering to lay flowers at a memorial outside the Royal Palace in Oslo.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a televised memorial address that his country was "united in grief and gratitude" for Harald's service and that his "legacy lives on".

The UK's King Charles III said he was mourning his "dear cousin". King Harald V was a second cousin of the King's mother, Queen Elizabeth II.

Haakon VIII is the great-great-great-grandson of Queen Victoria.

articles.title: South of France holiday scuppers Ed Davey's blood donation
articles.summary: The Lib Dem leader was unable to give blood due to visiting an area where there is the risk of mosquito-borne viruses.
articles.body:
A summer holiday to the south of France scuppered Sir Ed Davey's attempt to give blood to the NHS.

The Liberal Democrat leader had been poised to donate at the Brixton Donor Centre but, after filling out paperwork, was told he could not go ahead due to his recent trip to the Charente region.

The NHS says those returning from certain parts of France between May and November should wait four weeks before donating due to the risk of mosquito-borne viruses.

A Liberal Democrat spokesperson said Sir Ed would return to give blood once the 28 days had passed.

His visit to the south London centre was part of a campaign to promote blood donations to "beat the winter crisis" in the NHS.

NHS Blood Donation says it needs over 140,000 people to donate blood for the first time this year to meet demand. Blood has a shelf life of 35 days, so stocks need constant replenishing.

Earlier this year, the NHS warned it faced "a significant shortfall in blood stocks with hot weather, holidays and high demand all significantly impacting supplies".

Gerry Gogarth, director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant said: "We urgently need anyone eligible to donate to book an appointment as soon as they can."

Anyone wishing to donate blood can sign up on the NHS Blood Donation website, external or use the app to register and book an appointment.

There are restrictions on who can donate blood including limits on those who have recently travelled to particular areas.

In Sir Ed's case, the risk of exposure to ChikV and Dengue virus in parts of France prevented him from donating.

The French regions covered by the restriction are Bouches-du-Rhône, Charente, Dordogne, Hautes-Pyrénées, Haute-Garonne, Pyrénées-Orientales, Var, Gard, Hérault, Isere, Alpes-Maritimes, Vaucluse or Corsica.

A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "Ed unfortunately could not give blood today due to recent changes to rules regarding blood donations after travelling to certain destinations.

"Ed went to the Charente region in France on holiday which poses an infection risk due to mosquito prevalence, he will have to wait 28 days after returning home in order to give blood. He'll be back."

A charge of possession of a firearm had previously been authorised but was discontinued before the Crown Court hearing, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.

articles.title: Paul Heaton scores first number one album as Dolly Parton's 9 to 5 finally reaches top 40
articles.summary: Heaton's solo album tops the chart, while Parton's 1980 US hit reaches the UK top 40 at last.
articles.body:
English singer-songwriter Paul Heaton has scored his first solo UK number one album, his sixth overall.

Heaton's latest chart-topping LP - titled Jenius - follows his three with the Beautiful South and two more alongside former bandmate Jacqui Abbott.

The former Housemartins musician reached the top on Friday, in part, by shifting more vinyl copies than any other album over the past seven days.

Dolly Parton, who died earlier this week, aged 80 , has three singles in the top 40, including 9 to 5, which landed at number 12 in this week's UK chart, having previously peaked at 47 in 1981.

Elsewhere on Friday, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In extended its record as the longest-running number one single in UK chart history.

In a four-star review , the Times noted how Heaton's "casually funny" and "deceptively piercing" latest album "again confirms his gift for dissecting human weakness with an unsentimental but humane eye".

Victoria Segal wrote that the Ian Broudie-produced record was full of "stylistically playful songs" - like One Eye Open and Favourite Kind of Idiot - which "weave through the personal and political".

Heaton, who rose to fame as part of Hull band The Housemartins in the 1980s - alongside pre-Fatboy Slim Norman Cook - this week told the BBC he was planning on putting money behind the bar at dozens of pubs to celebrate his 65th birthday next year.

The singer made a similar gesture in 2022 when he opened £1,000 tabs at 60 pubs.

Fellow singer Brandon Flowers' pivot from the glamorous indie rock 'n' roll of The Killers to Parton's own brand of country music saw him land behind Heaton at number three, with his new album Thrasher.

Waves of tributes poured in this week to Tennessee star Parton, whose best-loved tunes were also played across the nation, evidently.

Her biggest streaming country-pop classic 9 to 5 was written for the 1980 film of the same name, and earned her an Oscar nomination as well as topping the US charts.

Another of her tunes, Jolene - which finds her pleading with a stunning rival not to steal her man - re-entered the chart at number nine on Friday.

The country anthem originally peaked at number seven in 1976 - her joint-highest UK chart placing.

Her duet with Kenny Rogers, Islands in the Stream, also reached number seven in 1983, and it has flowed back into this week's chart at number 13.

Finally, Diamonds & Rhinestones, Parton's 2022 greatest hits collection, reached the top 10 of the albums chart - topped by Heaton - for the first time too.

"Dolly Parton's extraordinary legacy continues to shine through the official charts," noted Becca Monahan and Chris Austin, co-managing directors of the official charts company, in a joint statement.

They called it a "powerful reflection of the UK's enduring love for her music".

"A true icon whose songs have crossed generations, these chart returns are a fitting celebration of Dolly's incredible life, career and lasting impact," they added.

articles.summary: Khalsa Aid International, based in Berkshire, is coordinating relief efforts on the ground in Nepal.
articles.body:
The chief executive of a Berkshire-based charity coordinating relief efforts in Nepal has described the flash floods as a "tragedy beyond words".

The floods struck on Wednesday after a glacier collapse triggered landslides and sent torrents of mud, water and debris downstream.

The number of people killed in Nepal has risen to 579, according to the latest release by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Officials say that around 4,000 people have been rescued.

Khalsa Aid International, based in Maidenhead, is providing emergency aid.

Chief executive Ravi Singh described it as a "very tough situation" and said they had got teams about to land in Nepal from India, with a focus on providing shelter.

"The locals in Nepal are stepping up, helping with food, water," he said.

"There are massive supplies coming from different areas and towns which are not affected."

He said one of the key challenges had been the mudslide, which had left a "huge area" covered in mud.

Singh said: "We didn't expect it. We know the people in Nepal very well. We were there 2015... it's deeply, deeply, sad.

"The tragedy is beyond words... and I think it shows the power of nature.

"Flash flooding is very, very powerful, very, very fast, and it's something that people don't realise. Once a flash flood hits, it takes everything with it."

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and, despite fears of a second wave of flooding , search efforts have continued.

Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.

The missing Britons are among hundreds of people unaccounted for, with rescue efforts continuing in the Rasuwa district, which borders China's Tibet Autonomous Region.

articles.body: H-1B visa holders in the US used to get a 60-day grace period to stay in the US once they lose their jobs. This grace period has been a cushion to help H-1B visa holders look for another job, figure out what to do next, change status to a tourist to continue staying in the US legally, or to change to H4 (spouse of H-1B) or F1 ( student visa) accordingly. The Donald Trump administration earlier announced that it will be doing away with the grace period; meaning H-1B visa holders will have to leave US if they lose their jobs and go back to their home country as they figure out what to do next. The proposal ha snow received a key approval of a White House office and will be released soon.Bloomberg reported that the Department of Homeland Security proposal (RIN: 1615-AD22) cleared review at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on Thursday.Indian-American entrepreneur Vivek Wadhwa said this is the scariest situation possible for H-1B visa workers. "It pushes them further into indentured servitude and gives unscrupulous employers even more leverage. It widens wage disparities, suppresses bargaining power, and hurts both H-1B and American workers. And Big Tech won't lobby against it; only strengthens their leverage," Wadhwa said.Immigration researcher Daniel Di Martino said companies will now prefer H-1Bs even more. "This proposed rule will make the H-1B visa more like indentured servitude because job changes will become more difficult. This undercuts the administration's stated goal of helping put Americans on a level playing field with foreign workers. Companies will prefer H-1B even more," he said."Not only do I personally think this will run into some legal hurdles, but all the people that complain about the H-1B program because “workers are much more willing to put up with whatever or have to leave” should be opposed to this regulation.
